extracted.intended_audience: NIH-funded and -applying biomedical researchers, PIs, program officers, and others interested in NIH grant policy and peer review
extracted.subtask_description: A commentary-style collection of evaluative statements and guidance about NIH grant review, funding decisions, scope changes, NOFO use, and related applicant/PO behaviors. Useful for PIs preparing proposals, interpreting NIH data, or navigating Program interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of scope (NIH GPS / NOT-OD-26-007)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change in the direction, aims, objectives, purposes, or type of research, identified in the approved project; this can include changes to Aims, Objectives, Titles, and Abstracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per NOT-OD-26-007: changes in scope become new terms and conditions of award, and the recipient must comply. Example: changing a Title is explicitly a change of scope. Treat proposed edits to Title/Abstract/Aims seriously — they may require formal negotiation/approval and create new compliance obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant is not a contract (PI flexibility vs Program oversight)
rubrics_metrics.description: The grant mechanism affords PIs flexibility to make progress under proposed Aims, but is not a contract guaranteeing unfettered changes; Program may object if PI veers 'too far' outside peer-reviewed scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect some latitude, but 'too far' is a slippery concept. If Program, grants management, or PO disagree with a substantive change in direction, you may need to negotiate or seek approvals; informal silence (e.g., PO not objecting to a one-line progress report mention) does not guarantee implicit approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documented animal-species and other explicit usage restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot spend grant funds on research using a vertebrate animal species not mentioned in the original proposal without doing required paperwork with OLAW and obtaining PO concurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under normal times this is a clear black-and-white example: make explicit protocol/species changes only after required approvals; failing to do so risks noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title/abstract wording changes can imply disallowed research angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests from Program to remove certain words (e.g., 'equity', 'diverse', 'racial', 'gender') from titles/abstracts are not necessarily cosmetic and may indicate Program does not want research pursued from particular angles or perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altering titles for 'form's sake' may still have real impacts. PIs asked to remove these words may legitimately fear constraints on the perspectives/angles they can pursue or potential future enforcement actions; treat such requests as substantive and consider implications before acquiescing.

rubrics_metrics.name: NOFO/FOA purpose and appropriate use
rubrics_metrics.description: NOFOs (Targeted Funding Opportunity Announcements) exist to address research needs not likely to be met by unsolicited applications — e.g., new pathogens, urgent questions, or under-studied populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cautions that NOFOs are often used belatedly, to prioritize topics politically, or to advantage certain investigators. ICs can also accomplish priorities by 'picking up' unsolicited grants; NOFOs are not the only mechanism. Be skeptical of claims that NOFO is strictly necessary to fund a topic; evaluate timing, target audience, and windows for submissions for possible favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program officers can and should balance portfolios (PO discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Program staff have the authority to pick up grants and balance portfolios; they are not completely constrained to follow peer review percentiles strictly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PIs should understand that Program may use discretion to fund lower-scoring but strategically important applications. Conversely, Program decisions may be influenced by political layers or by a desire to avoid controversy; monitoring PO behavior and portfolio choices is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review is subjective and panel composition matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Review outcomes are driven by attitudes of assigned reviewers and the panel; panels dominated by members from a particular IC or viewpoint will tend to favor proposals aligned with that interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect subjectivity: a panel that is 80% from IC-A will generally score IC-A-relevant proposals better. 'Appropriate competition' (grouping by science vs IC) does not guarantee fairer outcomes. For applicants: consider likely study section composition, choose study section/assignment strategically if possible, and be aware that reviewer mix affects scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: CSR consolidation and reviewer allocation implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Consolidation of review into CSR groups applications by science rather than by funding IC; CSR plans to create new chartered study sections and recruit prior IC reviewers to retain expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While this may reduce 'local variation in review practices,' it can also produce panels with different mixes of IC perspectives; overflow panels will be divided into scientifically coherent sets, and the practical effects should be monitored via rosters and funded grants to evaluate any systematic shifts in outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit payline and percentile-based funding probability
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'implicit payline' — the percentile score at which proposals are likely to be funded — can be estimated from NIH data (Report 302), and has varied across fiscal years (e.g., ~4%ile in FY2025 vs ~11%ile in FY2023).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report 302 charts can be used to estimate probability of funding by percentile, but beware limits: Report 302 excludes ND (Not Discussed) applications (triaged), and choice of including R56 awards affects rates. Use the underlying tables to calculate your own probabilities and compare across FYs and ICs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Funding Rate (per-PI) vs Success Rate (per-application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding Rate measures whether a PI who applied in a given FY received any award (per-PI), whereas Success Rate is per-application — these are different statistics and can convey different impressions of 'difficulty' of funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret NIH-provided statistics carefully; a headline 'funding rate' may understate per-application difficulty if prolific applicants submit many applications. For individual application strategy and expectation-setting, use per-application success rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triaging/Not Discussed (ND) skews denominators in public tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Some NIH reports (e.g., Report 302) include only applications that received a score; many R01-equivalent applications are triaged (ND) and therefore excluded from those denominators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When computing success probabilities or comparing FYs, include awareness of what the denominator is. If you use tables with only scored apps you will overestimate the apparent success rate compared with including triaged applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: NOFO/FOA drafting and 'right investigators' risk favoritism
rubrics_metrics.description: NOFOs sometimes specify narrow targets and short windows and are drafted with 'right investigators' in mind, which can advantage certain groups and create perceptions (or realities) of favoritism or 'scientific colonialism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to tight timelines and narrowly framed NOFOs as potential mechanisms that advantage established investigators; community scrutiny and transparency in NOFO timing/justification are warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic/area funding tradeoffs (portfolio tradeoffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any allocation of more funding to a particular disease/topic implies less funding to other areas — NIH prioritization is inherently a set of tradeoffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments for shifting portfolio resources should account for impacts elsewhere. PIs advocating for more funds in one area should be prepared to address which areas will receive less.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual evidence matters for evaluating reform claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about 'new' reforms or the need for novelty (e.g., reducing paperwork, funding younger investigators, funding new ideas) should be assessed against the long history of NIH programs and prior reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing or evaluating reforms, contextualize with NIH's prior programs (e.g., New Innovator, MIRA, MERIT, changes to A1/A2 policies) and data on outcomes; simplistic critiques may ignore existing mechanisms and tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious interpreting demographic outcome summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary statistics (e.g., 'BIPOC women had nearly three times higher odds of equity-related termination') can be misrepresented if taken out of context; careful reading of sampling frame and baseline rates is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using demographic odds/ratios, check denominators and base rates (e.g., whether analysis is among funded grants only), consider confounders (topic, FOA type), and avoid simplistic top-line summaries that misrepresent heterogeneous subgroup effects.
